paper_metadata.title: Effect of thermomechanical processing history on microstructural evolution and fracture mechanisms in NbTaTiHf refractory medium-entropy alloy

evidence.quote: This study examines how processing history governs microstructural evolution and tensile fracture behavior in the NbTaTiHf RMEA.
A comparison of the tensile properties of the NbTaTiHf RMEA across different processing histories reveals that the processing history exerts only a modest influence on strength
Senkov et al. [21] reported that the equiatomic NbTaTiHfZr alloy adopts a single-BCC structure both in the as-cast condition and after annealing above 1000 ◦C.
Zou et al. [33] examined an equiatomic NbTaMoW RMEA with a single BCC phase annealed at 1800 ◦C.
we successfully synthesized a single BCC-structured NbTaTiHf RMEA by cold-crucible induction melting

In single phase HEAs/MEAs, room-temperature mechanical behavior is typically governed by three classical strengthening mechanisms: solid-solution strengthening, work hardening, and grain-boundary (Hall–Petch) strengthening.
Work hardening, the increase in flow stress with plastic strain, arises from dislocation multiplication and interactions, reflecting a material's capacity for uniform plastic deformation.

In summary, the formation of kink bands rotating about the <110> axis in BCC HEA following hot rolling represents an alternative deformation mechanism activated to accommodate large plastic strains under conditions where conventional slip is impeded.
